def: Sealed stainless steel container, commonly 20, 30 or 50 litres, that holds pressurised beer for draught dispense. Kegs protect beer from light and air far better than open vessels.
Unfiltered ale that finishes conditioning in its cask and is served without added gas pressure, usually by hand pump. Once tapped it must be sold within days because air replaces the beer drawn off.
Aluminium container with a thin inner lining, sealed by a lid seamed onto the body. Cans block all light and weigh little, though filling must be tightly controlled to keep oxygen out.
Glass container for beer, most often brown because amber glass blocks most of the light that causes skunky flavour. Green and clear glass give little protection.
Glass bottle collected after use, washed and refilled. Common in Indian mass-market beer, it cuts packaging cost but needs careful inspection for chips, residue and scuffing.
Crimped metal cap that seals a beer bottle, with a liner that grips the glass. Some liners absorb oxygen, which helps slow staling in the bottle.
Level to which a bottle or can is filled, checked against the declared volume. Short fills shortchange the drinker and overfills waste beer, so lines check it every shift.
Gas space between the beer and the closure in a bottle or can. Air left there is a major source of package oxygen, so fillers work hard to push it out.
Tiny jet of hot water or CO2 squirted into a bottle just before capping so the beer foams up and drives air out of the headspace. It is a cheap way to cut oxygen pickup.
Oxygen dissolved in beer, measured in parts per billion (ppb). Keeping it low after fermentation is one of the biggest levers for flavour stability.
All the oxygen in a sealed package: the dissolved oxygen in the beer plus the oxygen in the headspace. It is the figure that best predicts how fast a packaged beer will stale.
Oxygen that gets into beer during transfers, centrifuging or packaging. Each step adds a little, so breweries measure before and after each one to find the leak.
Chemical reaction of beer compounds with oxygen that dulls hop aroma, darkens colour and creates stale flavours. Once it starts in the package it cannot be reversed.
Slow loss of fresh character as beer ages, driven by oxygen, heat and time. Hop aroma fades first; papery, honey or sherry notes follow.
How long a packaged beer stays within its intended flavour, set by the brewery from forced ageing and real-time tasting. Heat in Indian supply chains can shorten it sharply.
Date on a label up to which the producer expects the drink to keep its quality when stored as directed. It is a quality promise, not a safety cut-off.
Test that stores sealed beer warm, commonly at 30°C (86°F) or higher, for days or weeks to predict how it will taste months later on the shelf.
Damage caused when blue and ultraviolet light breaks down hop bitter compounds in beer, creating a skunky smell. In clear or green glass it can happen within minutes in sunlight.
Heating beer enough to kill spoilage organisms, giving a longer, more stable shelf life. Too much heat gives a cooked, bready flavour.
Measure of heat treatment where one unit equals one minute at 60°C (140°F). Breweries target a PU range that kills spoilage organisms without cooking the beer.
Long machine that sprays filled bottles or cans with water in warming, holding and cooling zones as they travel through. It treats the beer inside the sealed pack.
Removing soil, protein, beer stone and other deposits from a surface, usually with caustic or acid detergents. A surface must be clean before it can be sanitised.
Reducing microbes on an already clean surface to a safe level with chemicals such as peracetic acid or with hot water. Sanitising a dirty surface does little because soil shields bacteria.
Cleaning tanks and pipework by pumping detergent and rinse cycles through them without taking them apart. Time, temperature, concentration and flow together decide whether it works.
Regular flushing of beer lines, couplers and taps with line cleaner to remove yeast, bacteria and scale. Dirty lines are a common reason good beer tastes bad at the bar.
Weighted glass float that measures the density of wort or beer by how deep it sinks. Brewers use it to track fermentation and work out alcohol content.
Brewing scale giving the percentage by weight of dissolved extract in wort or beer, so 12°P means 12 g of extract per 100 g of liquid. Most commercial breweries record gravity this way.
Handheld instrument that reads sugar content from how much a drop of liquid bends light. It is quick for wort, but alcohol distorts readings once fermentation starts, so a correction is needed.
Lab instrument that measures how much light a sample absorbs at a set wavelength. Breweries use it for colour, bitterness units and other standard methods.
European Brewery Convention scale for beer and malt colour, read from light absorbance at 430 nm. EBC values are roughly double SRM values, which helps when comparing recipes.
Lab measure of bitterness made by extracting acidified beer with iso-octane and reading absorbance at 275 nm. It tracks bitter hop compounds, not how bitter a beer actually tastes.
Electronic probe that measures acidity. Brewers check pH in the brewhouse and in finished beer because it affects flavour, stability and microbial safety.
Any aroma or taste that does not belong in a beer or its style, caused by faults in ingredients, process, hygiene or packaging. Learning to name them is the core of brewery QC.
Cooked sweetcorn or tinned vegetable aroma from dimethyl sulphide, which forms from a precursor in pale malt. A weak boil or slow wort cooling leaves too much behind.
Buttery or butterscotch flavour from a compound yeast makes during fermentation and normally reabsorbs. Too much signals beer taken off yeast too early or a bacterial infection.
Green apple or freshly cut pumpkin flavour from a compound yeast makes on the way to alcohol. It points to young beer, stressed yeast or late oxygen pickup.
Clove, smoky, plastic or medicinal flavours from phenol compounds. Expected in hefeweizen and some Belgian ales, they are a fault elsewhere, often from wild yeast or chlorine.
Tinny, blood-like or coin-like taste, usually from iron or other metal ions picked up from water, worn equipment or poorly passivated stainless steel.
Stale flavours of wet cardboard, paper, honey or sherry that develop as beer reacts with oxygen. Hoppy beers also lose their aroma and can turn dull or darker.
Pungent smell like a skunk, burnt rubber or cannabis from 3-MBT, a sulphur compound formed when light hits hop compounds. Brown glass and cans prevent it.
Unwanted sourness from lactic or acetic acid bacteria, often with haze, ropiness or vinegar notes. It usually traces back to a hygiene gap in hoses, heat exchangers or packaging.
Rotten egg or struck match aroma from hydrogen sulphide and related compounds made by yeast. A trace in young lager often fades with conditioning; persistent sulphur suggests stressed yeast.
Cloudiness in beer from protein, polyphenols, yeast, starch or bacteria. Some styles want it; in a beer meant to be bright it is a stability fault.
Sensory test where tasters get three samples, two identical and one different, then must pick the odd one. It shows whether a process change makes a detectable difference.
Trained group of tasters who assess beer by agreed methods, checking flavour, faults and trueness to brand. Their scores are QC data, just like lab numbers.
Sensory check of whether a batch tastes as the brand should, judged against a fresh reference sample. It catches drift that lab numbers alone can miss.
Time-ordered plot of a measurement with a centre line and statistical control limits. Points outside the limits or unusual runs show a process has shifted and needs attention.
Packaging line score that multiplies availability, performance and quality into one percentage. It shows how much theoretical output actually becomes good, saleable product.
Printed code on a can, bottle or keg that ties it to a brew, tank and packaging run. Without it a recall or complaint investigation becomes guesswork.
What a beer smells like, sensed through the nose before and while drinking. Most of what people call taste is really aroma, so judges assess it first.
Chart that groups beer flavour terms from broad classes at the centre to specific descriptors at the rim. It gives tasters and brewers a shared vocabulary.
Fruity aromas such as banana, pear or apple made by yeast during fermentation. Wanted in many ales and wheat beers, they are usually kept low in clean lagers.
Physical sensations a beer gives in the mouth, such as body, carbonation, warmth, creaminess and astringency. It shapes how refreshing or rich a beer seems.
Perceived weight or fullness of a beer on the palate, from thin and watery to thick and chewy. Residual sugars, proteins and alcohol all add to it.
Flavours and sensations left after swallowing, described as short or long, dry or sweet, bitter or clean. A good finish invites the next sip.
Dry, puckering, tea-like roughness on the palate caused by tannins and other polyphenols. A little suits some roasty beers; too much usually points to harsh husk extraction.
Prickly, slightly acidic tingle on the tongue as dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid. Higher carbonation makes beer feel lighter and sharper; low carbonation feels softer and fuller.
How long the foam on a poured beer lasts before collapsing. Grease, detergent residue on glasses or poor foam proteins can kill it quickly.
Rings of foam that cling to the inside of the glass as the beer is drunk. Good lacing suggests healthy foam proteins and a properly cleaned glass.
Temperature at which a beer shows its best. Light lagers suit about 3 to 5°C (37 to 41°F), while strong dark ales open up nearer 10 to 13°C (50 to 55°F).
Percentage of a drink's volume that is pure ethanol. A 5% ABV beer contains 5 ml of alcohol in every 100 ml, which is how strengths are compared.
Measure of bitter hop compounds in beer, roughly milligrams of iso-alpha acids per litre. Malt sweetness changes how bitter the same number tastes.
American scale for beer colour, measured from light absorbance at 430 nm. Pale lagers sit around 2 to 4 while stouts reach 40 or more.
US non-profit that writes widely used beer style guidelines and certifies beer judges through tasting exams. Its guidelines are the reference at most homebrew competitions.
Certification programme for beer service and knowledge, running from Certified Beer Server up to Master Cicerone. It focuses on serving, storing, styles and food pairing.
London-based education body offering graded qualifications in wine, spirits, sake and beer through approved course providers worldwide, including in India.
Beer from smaller, independent breweries that prize flavour, variety and local character. India has no single legal definition, so the term is used loosely.
Beer fermented with bottom-fermenting lager yeast at cool temperatures, then cold-conditioned. Lagers are usually crisp and clean; most beer sold in India is lager.
Beer fermented with top-fermenting ale yeast at warmer temperatures, often 15 to 22°C (59 to 72°F). Ales tend to show more fruity esters than lagers.
Golden to amber ale of moderate strength with a balance of malt and hops. It is the parent of the IPA and a common flagship for new breweries.
Hop-forward pale beer with more bitterness and hop aroma than a standard pale ale. Born in England, it now spans English, West Coast, hazy and double versions.
American IPA that is clear, dry and assertively bitter, with piney, resinous and citrus hop character. It grew up in California and the Pacific Northwest.
Hazy, juicy IPA with soft bitterness, a full mouthfeel and heavy late hop additions. It stales quickly, so it is best drunk fresh and kept cold.
Stronger, more intensely hopped IPA, typically around 7.5 to 10% ABV. It needs extra malt to carry the hops without tasting harsh.
Crisp, dry IPA fermented with lager yeast at warmer temperatures, often with rice or maize in the grist. It pairs West Coast hop character with lager cleanness.
Dark, roasty ale made with roasted barley or dark malts, with coffee and dark chocolate flavours. Styles range from dry Irish stout to sweet milk stout and strong imperial versions.
Dark brown ale from 18th-century London with chocolate, caramel and toast flavours, usually softer in roast than stout. The line between the two has always been blurry.
Strong, rich, dark stout, often 8 to 12% ABV, with intense roast, dark fruit and chocolate notes. It was historically brewed in London for export to the Russian court.
Beer brewed with a large share of wheat, often half the grist or more, giving a soft body and good foam. Styles include hefeweizen, witbier and American wheat.
Unfiltered Bavarian wheat beer with banana and clove aromas from its special yeast. It is usually at least half wheat malt and served cloudy in a tall vase-shaped glass.
Dry, spicy, highly carbonated Belgian farmhouse ale with peppery and fruity yeast character. It was originally brewed for seasonal farm workers in Wallonia.
Any beer with deliberate tartness from lactic or acetic acid, made with bacteria such as Lactobacillus or Pediococcus or by blending. Methods range from quick kettle souring to years in barrels.
Spontaneously fermented wheat beer from the Brussels region, cooled in open vessels so wild microbes settle in, then aged in wooden barrels for months or years. It is tart, funky and usually still.
Blend of young and old lambic, bottled so the young beer referments and builds a lively sparkle. It is dry, sour and complex.
Tart German wheat beer brewed with salt and coriander, first from Goslar and later Leipzig. Light and refreshing, it suits hot weather.
Low-strength, very pale, sharply tart wheat beer from Berlin, often around 3% ABV. It was traditionally served with flavoured syrups to soften the acidity.
Pale, delicate beer from Cologne fermented with ale yeast at cool temperatures, then cold-conditioned. In Europe only Cologne-area brewers may use the name.
Pale, crisp, hop-accented lager first brewed in Plzen, Bohemia, in 1842. German versions are drier and more bitter; Czech versions are rounder and maltier.
Pale Munich lager that leans towards soft, bready malt rather than hop bitterness. Clean and gentle, it was created in 1894 as Bavaria's answer to pilsner.
Strong German lager, roughly 6 to 7.5% ABV, with rich toasty malt and little hop character. Doppelbock, maibock and eisbock are stronger or seasonal relatives.
Lower-alcohol beer, usually under about 5% ABV, built so several can be enjoyed in one sitting. A good one still needs flavour and balance.
Label word for a stronger, more intense version of a style, as in imperial stout or imperial IPA. It signals more malt, more alcohol and usually more of everything.
Beer matured in wooden barrels, often ex-bourbon, wine or rum, picking up vanilla, oak, spirit or wine notes. Ageing takes months and the wood can host souring microbes.
Beer served with a nitrogen and CO2 gas mix through a restrictor tap, giving tiny bubbles, a cascading pour and a creamy head. Dry stout is the classic example.
Restaurant or bar that brews beer on site and serves it there, usually straight from serving tanks. In several Indian states it is the main craft beer model.
Small brewery producing limited volumes, often with its own bar. In India the word often means an on-premise brewing licence; its exact meaning and rules vary by state.
Bar attached to a production brewery where its own beer is poured fresh. It earns the full retail margin and builds the brand directly with drinkers.
Arrangement where a brand owner pays an established brewery to brew and package its recipe. It lets brands launch without building a plant, though quality depends on the host.
Brewing by a brand or brewer with no plant of its own, renting spare capacity at other breweries batch by batch. It is a common way to test demand before investing.
Written contract between a brand owner and a host brewery setting out specifications, testing, sign-off and who pays for failed batches. It prevents arguments when a batch goes wrong.
Sales of drinks for consumption where they are bought, such as bars, pubs, restaurants and hotels. Margins and brand building work very differently here than in retail.
Sales of packaged drinks to take away and drink elsewhere, mainly through licensed liquor shops in India. Rules on who may sell vary by state.
Path a product takes from brewery to drinker through depots, distributors, wholesalers and retailers. In India state rules often decide who may buy from whom.
Tax charged by a state on alcohol made or sold within it, collected through permits, labels or volume-based charges. Structures and processes vary by state, so brewers need local advice.
Annual or one-off fee paid to the state for the right to brew, store or sell alcohol. Licence categories, fees and renewal cycles vary by state.
Document issued by the state excise department to move alcohol from a brewery to a warehouse, retailer or another state. Requirements and processes vary by state.
Store where alcohol is held under excise supervision before duty is paid. Duty usually falls due as stock leaves bond, though procedures vary by state.
Volume of a drink as measured, whatever its strength. Indian excise often counts beer in bulk litres and spirits in proof litres; methods vary by state.
Standard selling unit of packaged drinks, such as 12 bottles of 650 ml or 24 cans of 500 ml. Case sizes differ, so convert to litres before comparing sales.
Volume a brewery sends to distributors or depots, recorded at the factory gate. Shipments can rise while real consumer sales fall, so they are read alongside depletions.
Volume a distributor sells on to retailers and bars, a closer signal of real demand than brewery shipments. Comparing the two shows stock building up or running down in the trade.
Direct cost of making the product sold: ingredients, packaging, direct labour and production overheads. Companies treat excise differently within it, so check before comparing figures.
Total cost of making one litre of finished beer, including ingredients, packaging, energy, labour and overheads. Pricing and margin decisions should start from this number.
Revenue minus cost of goods sold, often shown as a percentage of revenue. It shows how much each sale contributes towards overheads and profit.
Highest price at which a packaged product may be sold to consumers in India, printed on the pack. For alcohol it is also shaped by state excise pricing rules.
Unit of 100 litres, the standard way breweries express batch size, tank volume and annual output. A 10 hl brewhouse makes about 1,000 litres per brew.
Volume of wort a brewhouse can produce per brew, usually given in hectolitres. Annual output also depends on brews per day and how much fermenting space follows.
Volume lost between brewhouse and sale through tank bottoms, filling waste, breakages and dumped batches. Tracking it stage by stage is one of the cheapest profit gains.
Core beer a brewery is best known for and sells all year round. Its steady volume usually pays for the seasonal experiments.

aka: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
def: India's national food regulator, which sets standards for alcoholic drinks covering composition, additives and labelling. Breweries need its licence alongside state excise approvals.
Process of getting a drink's label approved by the state excise department before sale. Each state reviews labels separately and requirements vary, so multi-state launches take time.
Day when the sale of alcohol is banned, such as certain national holidays, election days and some festivals. State governments set the dates, so taprooms plan stock and staff around them.
State where the sale and consumption of alcohol is prohibited, wholly or largely. Prohibition policies change over time, so check the current position state by state.
Scale of dissolved sugar in grape juice, where 1 degree equals 1 g of sucrose per 100 g of solution. Winemakers track it to time the harvest and predict potential alcohol.
Freshly crushed grape juice with its skins, seeds and pulp, before or during fermentation. Red wine takes its colour from fermenting with the skins in the must.
Conversion of sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid by bacteria, usually after the main ferment. It softens acidity and can add buttery notes to reds and some whites.
Dead yeast and other sediment that settle after fermentation. Ageing wine on its lees, called sur lie, adds texture and bready complexity.
Adding an agent such as bentonite, egg white or gelatin to wine so it binds haze-forming or harsh compounds that then settle out. Some agents make a wine unsuitable for vegans.
Polyphenols from grape skins, seeds, stems and oak that give red wine its drying grip. Tannin softens with age and helps a wine last.
Sulphur dioxide added to wine to protect it from oxidation and spoilage microbes. Most wines contain some, which is why many markets require a sulphite warning on the label.
Musty, damp cardboard smell caused by trichloroanisole, often from a contaminated cork. Even tiny amounts mute a wine's fruit.
Year the grapes were harvested, printed on many wine labels. Weather that year shapes quality, so vintage matters most in marginal climates.
Combined effect of site, soil, climate and slope on the character of a wine. It explains why the same grape tastes different from different vineyards.
Sparkling wine method where a second fermentation happens in the bottle, followed by ageing on lees, riddling and disgorging. Champagne is made this way.
Adding grape spirit to wine during or after fermentation, raising alcohol to roughly 15 to 22% ABV. Port, sherry and Madeira are made this way.
Fractional blending system of barrel tiers used for sherry, where wine for bottling comes from the oldest tier and is topped up from younger ones. Each bottle holds a little very old wine.
Film of yeast that grows on fino and manzanilla sherry in barrels left part full. It shields the wine from oxygen and gives a tangy, nutty, bread-dough character.
Wooden container, usually oak, used to mature spirits and wine. Ex-bourbon and ex-sherry casks are the most common for whisky, each shaping colour and flavour.
Time a spirit or wine spends ageing in cask, drawing flavour from the wood, oxidising gently and losing harsh notes. Heat speeds the process up.
Spirit lost to evaporation through the cask during maturation. Losses are far higher in hot climates such as India than in Scotland, which speeds ageing but costs volume.
Fermented liquid, much like an unhopped beer, that a distiller feeds into the still. For malt whisky it is usually around 7 to 9% ABV.
Clear spirit straight off the still before any cask ageing. Its quality sets the ceiling for the finished whisky.
Copper still run in batches, usually twice for malt whisky, giving a heavier, more flavourful spirit. The copper also strips out sulphur compounds.
Tall still that distils continuously over many internal plates, producing a lighter, stronger spirit efficiently. It is used for grain whisky, vodka and most Indian molasses spirit.
Moments when a distiller switches the spirit run from heads to hearts and from hearts to tails. Only the hearts are kept, so cut timing shapes flavour.
Highly rectified spirit of about 95 to 96% ABV with little flavour of its own. In India it is the base of most mass-market spirits, usually made from molasses or grain.
Older measure of alcohol strength. US proof is twice the ABV, so 40% ABV is 80 proof; British proof differs, with 100 proof equal to about 57.1% ABV.
Whisky made only from malted barley at a single distillery. Scotch single malt must also be distilled in pot stills and aged at least three years in oak.
Whisky made by mixing different whiskies, typically malt and grain. Many Indian blends also include neutral spirit, which is why labels and definitions differ by market.
Number on a whisky label giving the age of the youngest spirit in the bottle. A 12-year-old can contain older whisky but nothing younger.
Whisky bottled at the strength it comes out of the cask, without dilution with water, often above 50% ABV.
Partly decayed vegetation burned to dry malted barley, giving smoky, medicinal flavours measured in phenol parts per million. Islay whiskies are the best-known peated style.
Plant ingredients that flavour gin, led by juniper, which must dominate, plus coriander, citrus peel, angelica and many others. Indian gins often add local spices.
Gin method where botanicals sit in a basket above the boiling spirit so the rising vapour extracts their aroma. It gives a lighter, more delicate result than soaking the botanicals in the spirit.
Gin style where all flavour comes from botanicals distilled with the spirit, with only water and a trace of sugar allowed afterwards. The name describes a method, not a place.
Goan spirit distilled from fermented cashew apple juice or coconut palm toddy, traditionally in small pot stills. Cashew feni holds a geographical indication tag.
